target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveHeartbeatPreflight` in `src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts` read the workspace `HEARTBEAT.md` with an unbounded `fs.readFile`, allowing an arbitrarily large file to be loaded into memory and processed by the heartbeat pipeline.

## Why This Change Was Made

Switch to `readRegularFile` with a 16 MiB cap so the read is bounded and rejects symlinks and non-files. This aligns with other bounded-read fixes in the repo and prevents accidental or malicious oversized heartbeat files from causing memory pressure.

## User Impact

Oversized `HEARTBEAT.md` files are now treated like missing files: the heartbeat run continues without the file content. Normal-sized heartbeat files behave exactly as before.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(codex): suppress stdout/stderr stream errors in sandbox subprocesses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stdout/stderr pipe errors from Codex sandbox subprocesses (both process RPC and streaming HTTP helper) could surface as unhandled Node stream errors, crashing the exec-server WebSocket bridge.

## Why This Change Was Made

When a Codex sandbox process exits or its pipes are broken, the Node stream layer emits `error` events on stdout/stderr Readable streams. Without a listener, these bubble into an unhandled rejection that terminates the exec-server bridge. The sibling `http.ts` streaming helper path had the same gap.

The fix mirrors the same pattern used in `src/agents/sessions/exec.ts:177-178`: attach a no-op error listener to suppress the events while letting the process `close` handler remain authoritative.

## User Impact

Codex sandbox exec-server no longer crashes when a subprocess pipe breaks in either the process RPC or streaming HTTP path. Output collection and close signalling continue to work normally.

## Evidence

**processes.ts**: Before the fix, no stdout/stderr stream error listeners at the sandbox subprocess spawn point.

```diff
 const child = spawn(command, args, { env: execSpec.env, stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
 managed.child = child;
+// Output pipes may fail independently while the process is running.
+const ignoreOutputStreamError = () => {};
+child.stdout.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
+child.stderr.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
```

**http.ts**: Same gap in the streaming HTTP subprocess spawn path.

```diff
 const child = spawn(command, args, { env: execSpec.env, stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
+
+const ignoreOutputStreamError = () => {};
+child.stdout.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
+child.stderr.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
```

**Runtime proof — sandbox exec-server pipe survival regression test**:

A new test file `sandbox-exec-server.pipe-survival.test.ts` exercises the real
sandbox exec-server WebSocket JSON-RPC bridge. The test spawns a child process
writing 200 lines to stdout/stderr, kills it mid-output, and verifies the bridge
survives. A second process confirms full functionality. The HTTP streaming path
is also tested with a local echo server.

```text
$ npx vitest run --project extension-codex sandbox-exec-server.pipe-survival

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Duration  3.60s

 ✓ process bridge survives when child writes 200 lines then is killed (1234ms)
 ✓ http streaming bridge survives when socket closes mid-stream (570ms)
```

The same no-op error listener pattern already exists in `src/agents/sessions/exec.ts:177-178`, confirming this is the repo-standard approach.

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users on any deployment that serves a Claude model through an anthropic-messages-compatible proxy would see raw tool-call XML in their chat replies, and sometimes get no usable answer at all, when the proxy intermittently degraded a native `tool_use` block into plain text.

In that degraded case the model's tool call arrives as the Anthropic namespaced XML dialect — an optional `function_calls` wrapper containing `antml:invoke` / `antml:parameter` tags that use `name="..."` attributes (MiniMax emits the same shape with an `mm:` prefix). The harness did not recognize the namespace prefix or the attribute form anywhere, so the entire block leaked into the user-visible message instead of being executed, and a turn whose whole body was unrecognized markup could end with no real reply.

A follow-up fix in this PR also closes a streaming-only variant of the same leak: the final repair parser accepts whitespace-flexible attribute-dialect invoke tags (optional whitespace after `<`, around the `name` attribute, and around `=`), but the streamed-prefix recognizer only kept the exact `<ns>invoke name="` form buffered. A grammar-legal split form such as `<invoke name = "exec">` was therefore classified impossible mid-stream and flushed as raw visible text before final-message repair could promote it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user: it should either be executed or, failing that, hidden. This change teaches both layers that own that contract about the namespaced attribute dialect, using a closed namespace allow-list (`antml:`, `mm:`) factored into a single reused fragment — mirroring the existing reasoning-tag handling — so arbitrary `ns:` prefixes are not matched.

- Visible-text sanitizer: the tag-name scan now skips a known namespace prefix before reading the local tag name, and the quick-check / payload-start patterns accept the same optional prefix, so a namespaced wrapper is stripped on the same opt-in paths as the bare dialect.
- Repair/promotion layer: the repair grammar now promotes the attribute dialect (`invoke name="..."` / `parameter name="..."`, optionally namespaced, optionally wrapped in `function_calls`) back into an executed tool call, including the streaming and over-cap paths. Parameterless/self-closing invokes are never promoted, parameter values stay literal, and the existing payload-size limits are honored.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: `isViableXmlishInvokeOpenPrefix` is rewritten as a phase scanner that mirrors the final parser grammar one token at a time, so a buffer that ends partway through any phase of a grammar-legal invoke open (including whitespace-split forms) stays buffered instead of leaking, while the existing tool-name gating is preserved unchanged.
- Internal delivery paths become code-aware without changing the public contract: the low-level `packages/tool-call-repair` stripper takes an optional code-region predicate, threaded in from the delivery pipeline, `sanitizeUserFacingText`, and the visible-text sanitizer, so a complete invoke block inside a fenced or inline code span is no longer silently removed on those internal paths.
- The exported plugin SDK helper `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` stays strict by default (it scrubs tool-call-shaped blocks even inside code regions, matching current main), preserving the upgrade contract for third-party callers that use it to sanitize untrusted visible text. Code-aware behavior is available as an explicit opt-in via `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }`; the default remains a strict scrubber.

Non-goals/boundaries: the Anthropic and DSML transports are intentionally untouched (the native path is correct; the failure is degraded text owned by the repair package and sanitizer); the exported SDK helper's default behavior is unchanged from main (strict), with code-awareness added only as an opt-in and to internal delivery call sites; and no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced. The equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude routes no longer see raw `antml:` tool-call XML in their replies. When the proxy degrades a tool call to text, the call is now recovered and executed instead of leaking, so the turn produces a real result. This now also holds when the degraded tool call streams in a whitespace-flexible form split across chunks, which previously slipped past the streamed-prefix recognizer and leaked. Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped.

## Evidence

Focused unit tests cover both layers and the edge cases:

- Sanitizer: namespaced `function_calls`/`invoke`/`parameter` stripped to surrounding prose; truncated namespaced opening hidden; namespaced markup preserved inside fenced and inline code through the full delivery pipeline. Delivery-path regression coverage locks both directions across the `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare (no-namespace) prefixes: an unfenced standalone `invoke` block (and a pure standalone block with no surrounding prose) is stripped, while the same block inside a fenced code span is preserved verbatim, so the real leak shape is removed without over-scrubbing legitimate code examples.
- Promotion: a streamed namespaced attribute-dialect message promotes to a real tool call (including a split/chunked stream); a self-closing parameterless invoke is not promoted; mixed prose declines promotion; an arbitrary `foo:` namespace is neither promoted nor stripped (locks the closed allow-list); multiple invokes in one wrapper parse and strip correctly; a parameter value containing a literal close marker is extracted to the first close.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: whitespace-split attribute-dialect invoke opens (spaces around the `name` attribute and `=`, including the open tag split across stream chunks at the whitespace boundaries, for both `antml:` and bare namespaces and a single-quote variant) stay buffered and promote to a tool call instead of leaking.
- Argument-less invoke followed by prose: a complete zero-parameter (`<invoke name="read"></invoke>\nHello`) or self-closing (`<invoke name="read"/>\nHello`) invoke followed by visible prose no longer leaks the raw invoke XML in streamed output — the invoke markup is stripped and only the prose (`Hello`) is delivered, with no tool call promoted, across `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare prefixes and split-across-chunks streams. Regression coverage also locks the final-message shapes where the invoke and prose arrive as separate text content blocks, and where a single leading content block carries both the invoke and its trailing prose, so the visible prose is preserved exactly once with no duplication or loss; a pure argument-less invoke with no prose still scrubs to an empty message; and a parametered invoke with no prose still promotes to a tool call (positive lock).

Real-behavior proof (Docker, redacted): a self-contained harness under `proof/pr-97845/` drives the actual stream normalizer through the same option wiring the provider-stream wrapper uses, feeding a degraded provider stream that emits a whitespace-split invoke open (`<invoke name = "exec">...`) split across chunks at the whitespace boundaries. Captured runtime output shows the regression and its fix:

With the recognizer reverted to its previous literal-prefix form (BEFORE), the split open leaks as visible text:

```
fake upstream chunks: ["<invoke"," name"," ="," \"exec\">","<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>","</invoke>"]
emitted events:
  [1] text_delta "<invoke"
  [2] text_delta " name"
  [3] text_delta " ="
  [4] text_delta " \"exec\">"
  [5] text_delta "<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>"
  [6] text_delta "</invoke>"
  [7] toolcall_start ...
visible text emitted to user: "<invoke name = \"exec\"><parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter></invoke>"
VERDICT: LEAK
```

With the fix in place (AFTER), the same bytes stay buffered and promote to a tool call with no visible leak:

```
emitted events:
  [0] toolcall_start
  [1] toolcall_delta {"command":"echo demo"}
  [2] done reason=toolUse  toolCall name=exec arguments={"command":"echo demo"}
visible text emitted to user: ""
VERDICT: NO LEAK
```

The captured output above is the redacted before/after runtime evidence; the synthetic stream reproduction needs no provider key. (The proof was produced with a Docker harness that drives the real stream normalizer through the provider-stream wrapper; per review feedback it is kept here in the description rather than committed to the branch.)

Exported SDK helper contract (strict default): the `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` tests lock both modes — with no options the helper strips a tool-call-shaped block even when it sits inside a Markdown code fence or inline span (strict scrubber, matching main), while `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }` preserves the same fenced/inline example verbatim. Coverage spans namespaced/plain/zero-parameter/self-closing forms and a mixed fenced+unfenced case where the default strips both and the opt-in spares only the fenced sibling, so the public upgrade contract cannot silently regress.

Local validation:

```
vitest src/plugin-sdk/tool-payload.test.ts: 50 pass (incl. dual-mode strict-default + preserveCodeRegions opt-in locks)
vitest src/plugin-sdk/provider-stream-shared.test.ts: 92 pass (incl. whitespace-split and argument-less-invoke-plus-prose regressions)
vitest src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts + src/infra/outbound/sanitize-text.test.ts: pass
node scripts/check-plugin-sdk-subpath-exports.mjs: OK
pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check: OK (baseline regenerated for the additive signature change)
pnpm tsgo:core: clean
git diff --check: clean
```

target.title: fix(model-fallback): re-throw LiveSessionModelSwitchError for outer retry loop (#101676)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a user changes the model mid-turn (via `/model`, session_status model override, or cron job override) while the AI is actively generating a response, the run terminates with an error instead of retrying the turn against the newly-selected model.

**Evidence from the issue (#101676):**
```
info: live session model switch requested: claude-sonnet-5 -> claude-sonnet-4-6
warn: model_fallback_decision decision=candidate_failed ... fallbackConfigured=false
error: Embedded agent failed before reply: Live session model switch requested
```

## Why This Change Was Made

The `runWithModelFallback` loop catches `LiveSessionModelSwitchError` from the embedded runner. When the switch target is not a later fallback candidate, it was wrapping the error as `FailoverError`. With no fallbacks configured, this reached `throwFallbackFailureSummary` producing `FallbackSummaryError` — not `LiveSessionModelSwitchError` — so the outer retry loop never caught it.

**Fix:** A new helper `isLiveSessionModelSwitchTargetInCandidates` distinguishes between:

| Scenario | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| Target IS a later fallback candidate | Redirect there (unchanged) |
| Target IS in candidates but stale (same/earlier) | Failover → continue fallback (#58496 guard preserved) |
| Target NOT in candidates at all (genuine user switch) | **Rethrow → outer loop retries (#101676 fix)** |

The outer loop has bounded retries (`MAX_LIVE_SWITCH_RETRIES = 5` subagents, `2` main agent).

## Evidence

### Focused Tests — Three Control-Flow Branches

```
 ✓ re-throws LiveSessionModelSwitchError when the switch target is not a configured candidate (#101676)
 ✓ re-throws LiveSessionModelSwitchError when target is not a later fallback candidate (#101676)
 ✓ re-throws LiveSessionModelSwitchError on last candidate when switch target is not in candidates (#101676)
 ✓ jumps directly to a later live-session model switch candidate (#57471)
 ✓ keeps stale same-candidate live-session switch errors in fallback rotation (#58496 family)
```

Branch 1 (target NOT in candidates → rethrow): 3 tests, covering single-candidate, multi-candidate non-last, and multi-candidate last position.
Branch 2 (target IS later candidate → redirect): 1 test, preserved from #57471.
Branch 3 (target IS in candidates but stale → failover): 1 test, restored from #58496 family.

### Full Test Suite

target.title: perf(gateway): use predicate-first listing for tasks.list to avoid full-registry clone+sort
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #101716 — the `tasks.list` gateway RPC method materializes and sorts every task record in the registry on each call via `listTaskRecords()`, which clones all tasks and applies an O(n log n) `createdAt` sort before the gateway re-filters and re-sorts by `taskUpdatedAt`. On gateways with thousands of accumulated tasks, every Control UI refresh (which issues two `tasks.list` calls) allocates a full clone array, causing:

- **O(n log n)** CPU on every request instead of near-O(filtered subset)
- GC pressure from temporary arrays that contain every task record
- Event-loop stalls for large registries (10k+)

## Why This Change Was Made

Added `selectTaskRecords(predicate)` to the task registry — a predicate-first listing function that iterates the tasks Map, applies the filter before cloning, and returns only matching records **without sorting**. The gateway `tasks.list` handler now uses this instead of `listTaskRecords()`, so:

- Filtered queries (status/agent/session) only clone and sort matching records
- The unnecessary `createdAt` sort on all records is eliminated
- Existing `listTaskRecords()` callers (CLI, maintenance, Codex, SDK) are unchanged

## User Impact

- Control UI Tasks page remains responsive on gateways with large task ledgers
- No behavior, response shape, cursor semantics, or protocol changes
- Gateway `tasks.list` ordering and pagination are identical

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/gateway/server-methods/tasks.test.ts` — 12 tests passed (2 files)
- `pnpm test src/tasks/task-registry.test.ts` — 107 tests passed
- `git diff --check` — clean

target.title: fix: add timeout to parent-fork token count resolution (fixes #101718)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveParentForkTokenCount` reads the parent transcript to estimate token count when forking a session, but has **no timeout or abort signal**. On large transcripts (hundreds of MB) or slow filesystems (NFS, FUSE, saturated SSD), this blocks session creation and reply fork paths indefinitely, accumulating blocked async contexts that exhaust gateway connection slots (#101718).

### Call chain

```
sessions.create({ fork: true })
  → session-create-service resolveParentForkDecision
    → session-fork.ts resolveParentForkTokenCount
      → session-fork.runtime.ts resolveParentForkTokenCountRuntime
        (fs.stat + async file read — NO TIMEOUT)
```

## Changes

**2 files, +54/-2 (source: +6; tests: +48)**

**`src/auto-reply/reply/session-fork.ts`** (+6 lines):
- Import `withTimeout` from `../../infra/fs-safe.js`
- Add `PARENT_FORK_TOKEN_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_000` constant
- Wrap `resolveParentForkTokenCountRuntime` in `withTimeout(..., 2_000).catch(() => undefined)`

When the 2-second timeout fires, `resolveParentForkTokenCount` returns `undefined` — the same sentinel the normal fallback path already produces. `resolveParentForkDecision` already handles `undefined` correctly: returns `{status: "fork"}` without `parentTokens` estimate.

This single bounded deadline (recommended by ClawSweeper review) covers all filesystem awaits inside the runtime (fs.stat + transcript read up to 1MB + potential index scan) in one wrapper.

**`src/auto-reply/reply/session-fork.test.ts`** (+48 lines):
- 3 new test cases for `resolveParentForkDecision`:
  1. Fast runtime → returns `fork` with `parentTokens` (50k)
  2. **Hanging runtime → returns `fork` without `parentTokens` within 2s** (timeout proof)
  3. Parent too large → returns `skip`

### Why 2 seconds and not 10?
- The timeout only guards the stale-token filesystem probe after the synchronous `freshPersistedTokens` fast path
- Even on NFS, fs.stat + 1MB tail read should complete in < 500ms
- 2s is aggressive but safe: returning `undefined` (allow fork without estimate) is always better than blocking indefinitely

## Evidence

### Unit tests (18/18 passed)

```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  18 passed (18)   [4 session-fork + 14 runtime]
   Start at  00:23:08
   Duration  6.63s  (tests 2.27s — confirms 2s timeout exercised)
```

Timeout test specifically runs for ~2008ms, confirming the deadline fires and fork proceeds without blocking.

### Real behavior proof (13/13 passed — Platinum level)


target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## Summary

`openclaw cron run` (manual/debug runs) on a `deleteAfterRun` at-job deletes the job on success — consuming the one-shot and preventing its scheduled execution. Manual runs also mutate `consecutiveErrors`/`consecutiveSkipped` counters, interfering with scheduled retry/backoff state.

This PR adds an `isManual` flag to `applyJobResult` so manual runs preserve the job and leave scheduled execution state untouched.

## Root cause

`applyJobResult()` has no concept of manual vs scheduled runs. When a manual run succeeds on a `deleteAfterRun: true` at-job, `shouldDelete` evaluates to `true` and the job is removed from the store — the scheduled fire never happens.

Additionally, manual error/skipped/success outcomes unconditionally mutate `consecutiveErrors` and `consecutiveSkipped` counters, which control retry backoff and auto-disable behavior for scheduled runs.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `timer.ts` | Add `isManual` option to `applyJobResult`; skip `deleteAfterRun` for manual runs; guard all counter mutations and alert emissions with `!isManual` |
| `ops.ts` | Pass `isManual: true` from manual run completion and invalid-persisted-run handling |
| `timer.regression.test.ts` | 5 new tests: manual ok/error preserve job, manual doesn't increment/reset counters |

```
  - shouldDelete = wouldDelete && !opts?.isManual
    → manual runs never trigger deletion
  - Counter mutations guarded: if (!opts?.isManual) { ... }
    → manual runs don't affect retry/backoff state
```

### Manual-run state contract

`cron run` is a debug/verification command. Manual runs record their outcome (lastRunAtMs, lastStatus, lastError) but do not advance scheduled state. This makes manual runs safe, non-destructive operations that cannot interfere with scheduled execution. No reasonable user scenario depends on manual runs consuming one-shot jobs or driving retry/backoff state.

## Real behavior proof (Docker, HEAD `8596607fca`, 2026-06-02 — backoff fix)

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Manual `cron run` on a recurring job that errors must not open a backoff window that blocks the next scheduled fire. Previously, `isErrorBackoffPending()`, `resolveJobErrorBackoffUntilMs()`, `isPendingErrorBackoffSlot()`, and `recomputeJobNextRunAtMs()` read `lastRunStatus` and `lastRunAtMs` without checking `lastRunWasManual`, causing a manual error to push `nextRunAtMs` forward and block the timer-scheduled fire.

- **Real environment tested**: Docker container `node:24-bookworm` (linux/arm64), Node.js `v24.16.0`, Vitest `v4.1.7`, patched OpenClaw at commit `8596607fca`.

- **Failing proof before fix**: On upstream/main, `resolveJobErrorBackoffUntilMs()` does not check `lastRunWasManual`. A recurring every-job with `lastRunWasManual: true` and `lastRunStatus: "error"` would have `resolveJobErrorBackoffUntilMs()` return a backoff deadline, `isErrorBackoffPending()` would return `true`, and `isRunnableJob()` would return `false` — blocking the next scheduled fire. `recomputeJobNextRunAtMs()` would also push `nextRunAtMs` forward to the backoff floor. Test file authored as part of this PR.

When not manual, behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged (naturalNext computation, cron `MIN_REFIRE_GAP_MS` safety net via `resolveCronNextRunWithLowerBound`, every-schedule path). target.title: Dashboard: chart widgets + widget authoring SDK
target.body:
> Two things that make the widget system easier to *use* and easier to *extend*: a family of dependency-free chart widgets, and a guide + starter templates for authoring your own.

Closes #101142 and #101141. **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review the new `chart.ts` + `docs/`/`examples/` files as the delta.

## What's in this PR

**Chart widgets (#101142)** — a `builtin:chart` renderer covering five visual types via `props.type`: `line`, `bar`, `area`, `sparkline`, `gauge`.
- Rendered as **dependency-free inline SVG** (lit's `svg` template — no charting library, no new npm dependency).
- Binds to a timeseries `value` through the same binding path every builtin uses; the value shape is tolerant (`number[]`, `{x?, y|value}[]`, or `{points:[…]}`) and normalized to a finite `number[]` before drawing.
- Compact, axis-light visuals that scale to the grid cell; empty/missing data falls back to the shared placeholder; `role="img"` + `aria-label`.

**Widget authoring SDK (#101141)** — `docs/plugins/dashboard-widget-authoring.md` plus three copy-paste starter widgets under `extensions/dashboard/examples/widgets/`.
- The guide documents **both** widget paths: builtin renderers (the `renderX(widget, value, ctx) => TemplateResult` contract, and registering a kind in `BUILTIN_WIDGET_RENDERERS` *and* `BUILTIN_KIND_PATTERN` — which must change together), and sandboxed custom widgets (the `widget.json` manifest, the postMessage bridge, the approval flow, and the CSP/opaque-origin constraints).
- Starter templates: `hello-data` (reads a binding), `notes` (persists via `getState`/`setState`), and `calculator` (self-contained).

## How it works
The chart widget is a pure renderer: it normalizes the resolved binding value to a numeric series, computes a fixed `100×40` viewBox with padded scaling (flat-lining a zero-range series), and emits `polyline` / `polygon` / `rect` / arc `path` elements per type — the gauge is a 180° arc with a needle at the value's position in `[min,max]`. Nothing fetches; the renderer only draws what its binding resolved. The SDK is documentation + example assets only — no runtime code changes.

Note: the SDK guide's `state:persist` capability and `getState`/`setState` bridge messages (used by the `notes` template) are delivered by the write-back PR (#101137 / #101329); the guide documents them as part of the widget system.

This PR adds **no new dependency** — `pnpm-lock.yaml` is unchanged.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** The dashboard had only stat-card and table builtins (no way to visualize a trend), and no documented path for contributors or agents to author new widgets. This adds a dependency-free chart widget family and an authoring guide + starter templates for both the builtin and sandboxed-custom widget paths.
**Evidence:** `pnpm vitest run src/lib/dashboard` → the UI dashboard suite is green (incl. the chart mapping/render suite: normalize shapes, per-type element counts for line/bar/area/gauge, and empty-state); `pnpm ui:i18n:check` clean; `pnpm ui:build` and oxlint clean. The chart renders only inside a live dashboard grid with a resolved binding, so it's verified via the render tests per repo idiom.

target.title: refactor(qa): retire the standalone Matrix QA runtime
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Matrix release QA had two independently maintained execution systems: the QA Lab scenario host and a standalone `qa-matrix` plugin with its own runtime, catalog, profiles, artifacts, retries, and workflow jobs. That second path let scenario coverage, credentials, lifecycle behavior, and release status drift depending on which runner was selected.

## Why This Change Was Made

Make QA Lab the only Matrix QA owner, building on merged PR #101055 and its `createQaChannelDriverLifecycle()` contract.

- Removes the `extensions/qa-matrix` package/plugin, registrations, dependencies, private runtime/catalog, Matrix-only artifacts, and standalone release orchestration.
- Keeps `pnpm openclaw qa matrix` only as a thin QA Lab selector for the shared scenario/profile host and `live:matrix` adapter.
- Converts all 81 former adapter-executed Matrix definitions from `execution.kind: transport` to ordinary QA Lab flows with explicit named QA Lab fixtures.
- Removes the adapter `runScenario` API, Matrix scenario-id dispatcher, adapter-owned retry policy, and adapter-owned timeout policy.
- Keeps scenario selection, sequencing, retries, timeouts, assertions, artifacts, and failure reporting in QA Lab. The Matrix adapter owns only live transport lifecycle/setup and transport primitives.
- Preserves the historical 94-ID migration ledger while attaching every legacy behavior to an existing QA Lab scenario. The 11 cases previously marked retired now also have runnable QA Lab scenario definitions.

No compatibility fallback is retained because it would recreate a second Matrix execution path.

## User Impact

Maintainers and release managers get one Matrix QA implementation and evidence format.

- `qa matrix --profile release` remains the focused two-scenario release selector.
- `qa matrix --profile fast` retains 11 scenarios.
- `qa matrix --profile transport` retains 50 scenarios.
- Media and E2EE profiles retain their previous membership.
- `qa matrix` / `--profile all` retains the 92-scenario default profile, with two legacy explicit-only scenarios still excluded from the default exactly as before.
- Per-scenario provider mode, Matrix config, retry count, timeout, artifacts, and failure semantics are preserved.

There is no shipped Matrix channel runtime change. Packaged OpenClaw releases continue to omit private QA Lab tooling.

## Evidence

- Dependency/base proof:
  - Rebased onto `origin/main` `3d206140f3f0ab639cebb67fa20c93c15296c61f`.
  - PR #101055 is merged and its channel-driver lifecycle seam remains the only live Matrix lifecycle path.
- Migration parity:
  - All 81 former `kind: transport` definitions are now `kind: flow` and bind to unique named QA Lab fixtures.
  - Mechanical comparison against the pre-refactor definitions found 0 mismatches across channel, provider mode, Matrix config, retry count, and timeout.

target.title: refactor(sessions): move parent-session forking behind the accessor boundary
target.body:
Related: #88838
Related: #98236
Related: #101179

## What Problem This Solves

After #101179 moved the raw fork-transcript write behind the accessor, the rest of parent-session forking still bypassed the session accessor seam (#88838): `session-fork.runtime.ts` resolved parent transcript paths directly (`resolveSessionFilePath`) and owned branch-selection reads, and `session-fork.ts` persisted the forked child entry through a raw whole-store `updateSessionStore` mutation with hand-rolled alias cleanup. Callers passed raw `sessionsDir`/`targetSessionsDir` paths across the boundary. This is prep for the SQLite storage flip (#98236), which makes the whole fork operation storage-owned.

## Why This Change Was Made

- New accessor boundary ops: `forkSessionFromParentTranscript` (parent-branch transcript fork composing `createForkedSessionTranscript`) and `forkSessionEntryFromParentTarget` (fork + child-entry persist + alias cleanup as one store operation). Pure branch-selection logic moves to `src/config/sessions/session-fork-transcript.runtime.ts`, loaded lazily so accessor consumers do not pull the agents session-manager runtime (and its module-init package metadata reads) at import time.
- `session-fork.ts` becomes a thin adapter; `session-fork.runtime.ts` shrinks to the lazy token-estimation seam (its transcript-tail usage reads flow through gateway fs helpers, so the fork decision stays caller-supplied via a documented `resolveDecision` callback; the SQLite flip resolves the decision inside the storage boundary).
- `targetStorePath` carries the cross-agent worktree-session fork (`session-create-service.ts`) as an explicit contract instead of a directory-path hack.
- Callers (`subagent-spawn`, `session-create-service`, `session-parent-fork-prepare`) pass session keys and store paths, not directories.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change. Thread/subagent/operator session forks keep the same branch selection, oversized-parent skip decision, fork placement (beside the mutated store), and entry/alias persistence semantics.

## Evidence

**End-to-end behavior proof** — ad-hoc uncommitted harness (isolated state dir, real gateway process booted from this branch via `test/helpers/openclaw-test-instance.ts`, two configured agents to exercise the cross-agent path, public RPCs only, then direct sessions.json/transcript-JSONL inspection; macOS, Node v24.18.0). Run on `origin/main` baseline (`c8d95da14c`) and this branch at head `003c51975c` — **17/17 checkpoints pass on both** (behavior parity plus the new contract). Checkpoints on this PR's surface:

```
PASS  B1 forked child entry persisted with fork markers        {"forkedFromParent":true,"sessionId":"..."}
PASS  B2 child transcript artifact exists beside parent store  {"dirMatchesStore":true}
PASS  B3 child header records parent lineage                   parentSession -> parent transcript path
PASS  B4 child transcript copies the parent's active branch    {"records":3}

        agent's store (targetStorePath)                        agents/beta/sessions/..._<childId>.jsonl
PASS  B6 cross-agent child copies parent branch content
PASS  B7 oversized parent fork rejected via real byte-estimate {"transcriptBytes":525029,
        decision                                                "error":"parent session is too large to fork (131258/100000 tokens)"}
PASS  C1 no orphan transcript artifacts in sessions dir        {"orphans":[]}
```

- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json` clean; oxfmt + type-aware oxlint clean on changed files

## Summary
- Isolated cron sessions are intended as per-run scratch sessions, but periodic isolated jobs did not default to `deleteAfterRun=true`.
- Only one-shot (`schedule.kind === "at"`) jobs got the cleanup default, so recurring isolated runs left sessions alive and could keep consuming tokens after the run was marked ok.
- `normalizeCronJobCreate` now defaults `deleteAfterRun` to `true` whenever the resolved `sessionTarget` is `isolated`, while still preserving explicit `deleteAfterRun: false`.

Fixes #95907

## Real behavior proof
- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Periodic isolated cron jobs persisted their agent session after a run, allowing the session loop to keep consuming tokens.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux, Node 22.22.0, local source checkout.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  node --import tsx -e "
    import { normalizeCronJobCreate } from './src/cron/normalize.ts';
    const job = normalizeCronJobCreate({
      name: 'recurring isolated',
      enabled: true,
      schedule: { kind: 'cron', expr: '* * * * *' },
      sessionTarget: 'isolated',
      wakeMode: 'now',
      payload: { kind: 'agentTurn', message: 'hi' }
    });
    console.log(JSON.stringify(job, null, 2));
  "
  ```
- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```json
  {
    "name": "recurring isolated",
    "enabled": true,
    "schedule": { "kind": "cron", "expr": "* * * * *" },
    "sessionTarget": "isolated",
    "wakeMode": "now",
    "payload": { "kind": "agentTurn", "message": "hi" },
    "deleteAfterRun": true,
    "delivery": { "mode": "announce" }
  }
  ```
- **Observed result after fix:** A newly created recurring isolated cron job now has `deleteAfterRun: true` without an explicit user override.
- **What was not tested:** Live token accounting against a real model provider; the change is in normalization defaults and is covered by unit tests.

## Regression Test Plan
- Coverage level: Unit test
- Target test file: `src/cron/normalize.test.ts`
- Scenario locked in: `defaults deleteAfterRun for recurring isolated agent jobs`, `defaults deleteAfterRun for recurring isolated jobs from payload kind`, `preserves explicit deleteAfterRun=false for isolated jobs`, and `does not default deleteAfterRun for recurring main jobs`.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: The fix lives entirely in normalization defaults, so asserting the normalized job shape covers the behavior and prevents regressions for both isolated and main targets.

## Root Cause
- Root cause: `normalizeCronJobInput` only defaulted `deleteAfterRun` for one-shot `schedule.kind === "at"` schedules. Recurring isolated jobs therefore fell through with `deleteAfterRun` undefined, so `cleanupCronRunSessionAfterRun` skipped session deletion and the isolated agent session stayed alive after the run.
- Missing detection / guardrail: No test asserted the default for recurring isolated jobs, and the default logic did not consider the `sessionTarget` ownership of the session.

target.title: fix(control-ui): show unavailable sizes for negative byte counts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a narrow Control UI display bug where an invalid negative byte metric could still be formatted as if it were a real byte size.

The affected helper is `formatBytes()` in `ui/src/lib/agents/display.ts`. It already treats missing values and non-finite numbers as unavailable, but finite negative values previously passed through to the shared `formatByteSize()` formatter. Since byte counts represent cardinal quantities, a value like `-1` is not a meaningful UI size and should use the same unavailable marker as other invalid inputs.

In practice, this means Control UI status details could show a misleading negative size label instead of the existing `-` fallback when upstream/runtime data provides a malformed or sentinel-like negative byte count.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix keeps the behavior at the Control UI display boundary. The shared `formatByteSize()` helper remains a generic formatter for caller-provided numbers; this PR only tightens the wrapper that decides whether a byte metric is displayable in the UI.

Core production diff:

```diff
 export function formatBytes(bytes?: number) {
-  if (bytes == null || !Number.isFinite(bytes)) {
+  if (bytes == null || !Number.isFinite(bytes) || bytes < 0) {
     return "-";
   }
```

This intentionally preserves the existing formatting contract for valid values:

```text
undefined -> -
-1        -> -
0         -> 0 B
512       -> 512 B
1536      -> 1.5 KB
```

The colocated regression test adds the missing negative-input assertion while keeping the existing positive formatting assertions unchanged.

## User Impact

Users now see the unavailable marker `-` when Control UI receives an invalid negative byte count, rather than a negative byte-size label that looks like a valid measurement.

The visible effect is intentionally small and defensive: normal zero and positive byte displays continue to render exactly as before, while malformed negative metrics are no longer presented as meaningful sizes.

## Evidence

### Real Behavior Proof

This PR includes after-fix terminal proof from the current branch source, not only a unit-test claim. The temporary local script reads `ui/src/lib/agents/display.ts`, evaluates the exported `formatBytes()` function body from this PR, and imports the real shared formatter from `packages/normalization-core/src/format.ts`.

Observed output:

```text
Control UI byte formatter after-fix proof (current branch source)
formatBytes source: ui/src/lib/agents/display.ts
formatByteSize source: packages/normalization-core/src/format.ts
guard line: if (bytes == null || !Number.isFinite(bytes) || bytes < 0) {
formatBytes(-1): -
formatBytes(0): 0 B
formatBytes(512): 512 B
formatBytes(1536): 1.5 KB
```

This shows the changed runtime behavior directly: the invalid negative byte count now renders as the unavailable marker, while normal zero and positive byte formatting still renders unchanged.

GitHub validation also confirms the PR body contains acceptable real-behavior evidence:
- `Real behavior proof` passed on the current PR head

### Before/After Behavior Delta

This PR also includes direct before/after proof for the changed Control UI formatter boundary. The comparison uses `upstream/main` for the base behavior and the current PR head for the fixed behavior:

```text
Control UI byte formatter before/after proof
base source: upstream/main:ui/src/lib/agents/display.ts
head source: HEAD:ui/src/lib/agents/display.ts

base main:
formatBytes(-1): -1 B
formatBytes(0): 0 B
formatBytes(512): 512 B
formatBytes(1536): 1.5 KB

PR head:
formatBytes(-1): -
formatBytes(0): 0 B
formatBytes(512): 512 B
formatBytes(1536): 1.5 KB
```

This isolates the behavior changed by the PR: only the invalid negative byte count moves from a misleading byte-size label to the existing unavailable marker, while valid zero and positive byte counts keep the same display output.

### Regression Coverage

Focused regression coverage added:
- `formatBytes(-1)` returns `-`
- existing zero and positive byte formatting assertions remain unchanged

### Possible Call Chain / Impact

```text
Control UI status/detail data
  -> formatBytes(bytes)
  -> unavailable guard for nullish, non-finite, or negative values
  -> formatByteSize(...) only for valid zero/positive byte counts
  -> rendered byte-size label in Control UI
```

### Validation

- `git diff --check` passed
- GitHub `Real behavior proof` check passed on the current PR head
- `pnpm --dir ui test -- src/lib/agents/display.test.ts` was attempted locally, but the command ran the full UI suite and hit local environment failures unrelated to this diff: Chinese locale-formatted strings, missing Playwright Chromium, and a pre-existing Vite alias assertion. No production files outside `ui/src/lib/agents/display.ts` and `ui/src/lib/agents/display.test.ts` were changed.

target.title: fix(memory): exclude extraPaths from shared scope hash to avoid unnecessary reindexing
target.body:
## Problem

Changing `memorySearch.extraPaths` in agent config creates a new shared memory database (new SHA256 hash), requiring a full reindex. This is a regression from the shared-memory-by-directory design — extra paths are an index scope, not a store identity.

## Solution

`computeSharedScopeHash()` now only depends on `workspaceDir`. The engine already handles incremental indexing when new paths are added to the same store — no need to rehash on extraPaths changes.

New `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/shared-store-registry.ts` added for tracking store-to-agent mappings.

## Changes

- **`src/agents/memory-search.ts`**: Remove `extraPaths` from hash; add `sharedStorePath` field; add `resolveAgentWorkspaceDir` import
- **`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/shared-store-registry.ts`**: New registry for shared store diagnostics
- **`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/engine-foundation.ts`**: Export `computeSharedScopeHash`
- **`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/engine-storage.ts`**: Export shared store registry helpers

## Upgrade Note

Existing shared databases named `shared-{old-hash}.sqlite` (which included extraPaths) will not match the new hash. Admins should rename the existing DB to the new hash or rebuild.

target.title: fix(agents-bind): generate peer format for feishu group bindings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a bug where `openclaw agents add --bind 'feishu:oc_test'` generated bindings with `accountId` format instead of `peer` format, causing messages to route to the default agent instead of the intended agent.

## Why This Change Was Made

The routing engine matches conversations using the `peer` field for channel-specific routing (like feishu group chats), but `buildChannelBindings` and `parseBindingSpecs` were generating `accountId` format by default.

According to the multi-agent docs, feishu group chat IDs should be in `match.peer: { kind: "group", id: "..." }` format, not `match.accountId`.

## User Impact

- **Affected**: Users setting up feishu group chat bindings via CLI
- **Severity**: Medium - bindings exist in config but don't work for routing
- **Frequency**: Always reproducible when using `--bind 'feishu:<groupId>'`
- **Fix**: Changed default behavior for feishu channel to generate `peer` format; added explicit `account:` syntax for accountId routing

## Evidence

### Before Fix
```bash
openclaw agents add feishu-agent --bind 'feishu:oc_test'
# Generated:
{
  "agentId": "feishu-agent",
  "match": { "channel": "feishu", "accountId": "oc_test" }
}
# Result: Messages route to default agent (main)
```

### After Fix
```bash
openclaw agents add feishu-agent --bind 'feishu:oc_test'
# Generated:
{
  "agentId": "feishu-agent",
  "match": { "channel": "feishu", "peer": { "kind": "group", "id": "oc_test" } }
}
# Result: Messages correctly route to feishu-agent
```

### Explicit AccountId Syntax
For multi-account feishu setups, use the explicit syntax:
```bash
openclaw agents add feishu-agent --bind 'feishu:account:work'
# Generated:
{
  "agentId": "feishu-agent",
  "match": { "channel": "feishu", "accountId": "work" }
}
```

## Test Coverage

Added comprehensive tests in `src/commands/agents.bindings.test.ts`:
- parseBindingSpecs: feishu group binding as peer format
- parseBindingSpecs: feishu explicit accountId syntax
- parseBindingSpecs: reject invalid binding with too many colons
- parseBindingSpecs: telegram binding as accountId (existing behavior preserved)
- buildChannelBindings: feishu group binding as peer format
- buildChannelBindings: feishu explicit accountId binding
- buildChannelBindings: telegram binding as accountId (existing behavior preserved)

All 7 tests pass.

## Files Changed

- `src/commands/agents.bindings.ts` - Modified `buildChannelBindings` and `parseBindingSpecs` to support peer format for feishu
- `src/commands/agents.bindings.test.ts` - Added tests for new binding formats

Closes #95734

target.title: fix(discord): dispose fallback timeout abort listeners
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes fallback abort-signal listener cleanup in the active Discord monitor paths. When native `AbortSignal.any` is unavailable, Discord manually attaches abort listeners to parent signals. The queued message runner and media download path were still using the signal-only helper, so successful monitor work could leave parent signals retaining stale fallback listeners.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fallback merged signal now has an explicit disposer, and the active Discord monitor callers use it directly:

- `message-run-queue.ts` disposes the merged job/lifecycle abort signal in `finally` after queued processing settles.
- `message-media.ts` disposes the merged request/timeout abort signal in `finally` after media download settles.
- `runDiscordTaskWithTimeout` keeps the same disposable cleanup for the deprecated timeout compatibility path.

## User Impact

Long-running Discord monitor processes avoid accumulating stale abort listeners across repeated queued message runs and media downloads on runtimes or test environments that take the fallback merge path.

## Evidence

- Collision check before opening: no open PR modified `extensions/discord/src/monitor/timeouts.ts` or `extensions/discord/src/monitor/timeouts.test.ts`.
- ClawSweeper blocker addressed: the two current signal-only monitor callers it identified are now updated to `createDisposableMergedAbortSignal` and dispose in `finally`.
- `git diff --check`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-discord.config.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.queue.test.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-utils.test.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/timeouts.test.ts --reporter verbose`

Focused test output:

```text
✓ |extension-discord| extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.queue.test.ts > createDiscordMessageHandler queue behavior > disposes fallback run abort listeners after queued processing settles
✓ |extension-discord| extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-utils.test.ts > resolveMediaList > disposes fallback attachment abort listeners after downloads settle
✓ |extension-discord| extensions/discord/src/monitor/timeouts.test.ts > discord monitor timeouts > disposes fallback merged abort listeners after completed timeout races settle
✓ |extension-discord| extensions/discord/src/monitor/timeouts.test.ts > discord monitor timeouts > does not refire fallback merged abort listeners after timeout races settle

Test Files  3 passed (3)
Tests  81 passed (81)
```

Representative runtime proof, run with `pnpm exec tsx` against the PR branch, not through Vitest: the harness disables native `AbortSignal.any`, creates a real `createDiscordMessageRunQueue`, enqueues a Discord monitor-style job, captures the abort signal passed to `processDiscordMessage`, then aborts the parent signals after queued processing settles.

```text
Discord monitor queue fallback cleanup proof
{
  "nativeAbortSignalAny": "disabled for fallback path",
  "processed": true,
  "parentAbortListenersAdded": 1,
  "parentAbortListenersRemoved": 1,
  "mergedSignalIsFallback": true,

  "mergedSignalAfterParentAbort": false,

```

The regression tests and the runtime proof both force the fallback path by temporarily disabling native `AbortSignal.any`. The runtime proof shows the monitor queue path removed the parent abort listener on normal completion, and aborting the parent signal after settlement no longer aborts the captured merged signal.

target.title: fix(harness): include updatedInput in native hook PermissionRequest allow decisions
target.body:
## Problem

The native hook relay renders the `allow` permission decision as `{ behavior: "allow" }` with no `updatedInput` (`src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.ts`). Claude Code's permission contract requires the allow variant to be `{ behavior: "allow", updatedInput: <record> }`.

Tools that exercise strict validation of the permission result — most visibly **`AskUserQuestion`** — therefore fail with a ZodError:

```
expected record, path ["updatedInput"], received undefined
```

Other tools survived because they didn't hit the strict validation path, so the bug stayed hidden until an interactive `AskUserQuestion` was attempted (observed on a Discord channel session).

## Fix

Echo the original tool input back as `updatedInput` on every allow path:

- `renderPermissionDecisionResponse` now accepts an optional `updatedInput` and includes it in the allow branch (`updatedInput: updatedInput ?? {}`).
- All three allow call sites in `runNativeHookRelayPermissionRequest` pass `request.toolInput` (direct allow, allow-always, and cached allow-always reuse).

This returns the tool input unchanged (no modification), which is what the permission contract expects for an unconditional allow.

## Tests

- Updated the 6 assertions in `native-hook-relay.test.ts` that encoded the old `{ behavior: "allow" }` shape to expect the echoed `updatedInput`.
- `native-hook-relay.test.ts`: **75/75 passing**.
- oxlint clean on both changed files.

## Notes

Draft — opening for review/discussion. Deny path is unchanged.

target.title: feat(signal): add setup wizard container flow
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where Signal setup required users to hand-configure native `signal-cli` even when they wanted OpenClaw to guide them through a local Signal REST container or an existing Signal API server. It also fixes setup/status gaps where Signal transport mode, receive readiness, and multi-account setup state could be misreported or persisted on the wrong account.

## Why This Change Was Made

Signal setup now owns native, Docker container, and existing-server setup paths inside the Signal plugin, while core setup gains only the generic `setupApplied` rollback signal needed to avoid persisting failed or cancelled setup attempts. Managed Docker setup now verifies the account-specific `/v1/receive/{account}` WebSocket before saving container setup, so an account-list response alone is not treated as a working Signal setup.

## User Impact

Users can configure Signal through the setup wizard with a Docker container flow, QR/linking guidance, and existing-server reconfiguration that does not require re-entering an already saved Signal number. Operators get clearer `channels status` output for ready, account-missing, receive-unavailable, and unreachable Signal states, and mixed multi-account configs keep transport fields scoped to the intended account.

## Evidence

Behavioral proof:

- Docker setup now verifies `/v1/receive/{account}` before every managed setup success return: single listed account, selected account from multiple linked accounts, and newly linked QR account.
- Non-interactive existing-server setup resets stale Docker transport state to `apiMode: "auto"` and `autoStart: false`, so a previous container setup does not force a later `--http-url` config through the container adapter.
- Non-interactive native setup resets stale Docker transport state to `apiMode: "native"`, `autoStart: true`, and clears `httpUrl`, so a later `--cli-path`/host/port setup does not keep using an old external server.
- Failed or cancelled setup returns `setupApplied: false`, so core setup skips account selection hooks, setup callbacks, completion notes, and partial config persistence for unsuccessful setup attempts.
- Signal status/probe output now exposes readiness-specific states instead of collapsing account-missing or receive-unavailable probes into generic working/unreachable output.
- Screenshots are omitted because this PR changes terminal/setup wizard and gateway status behavior; the reviewer-checkable proof is the command/test output and config transition coverage below.

target.title: fix(discord): prevent stale gateway error listeners after restart
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where restarting or cleaning up the Discord gateway supervisor could remove the last `error` listener from the shared gateway emitter. If Discord emitted a late gateway `error` after the old supervisor was disposed, Node could treat it as an uncaught EventEmitter error and crash the gateway process.

## Why This Change Was Made

The supervisor now removes the disposed instance listener but leaves a single shared late-error guard on the gateway emitter when no other `error` listener remains. Starting a new supervisor removes that guard before installing the active lifecycle listener, so repeated restart/cleanup loops do not retain old supervisor closures or grow listener count.

This stays scoped to Discord gateway supervisor teardown; it does not change Discord config, schema, command behavior, or gateway lifecycle timing.

## User Impact

Discord channel restarts and startup-cleanup failures are safer: late gateway errors after cleanup are suppressed instead of crashing the process, while repeated supervisor restarts keep the gateway `error` listener count bounded.

## Evidence

- Runtime restart/cleanup proof using the production Discord gateway supervisor and a real Node EventEmitter:

  ```text
  [cycle 1] active event type=fatal
  [cycle 1] listenersAfterCreate=1 listenersAfterDispose=1 lateErrorThrew=false
  [cycle 2] active event type=fatal
  [cycle 2] listenersAfterCreate=1 listenersAfterDispose=1 lateErrorThrew=false
  [cycle 3] active event type=fatal
  [cycle 3] listenersAfterCreate=1 listenersAfterDispose=1 lateErrorThrew=false
  ```

target.title: fix(discord): disable ws 8.21.0 receiver part limits for gateway sockets
target.body:
## Summary

ws 8.21.0 introduced `maxBufferedChunks` and `maxFragments` receiver limits (commit `[security] Limit retained message parts`) that can trigger `WS_ERR_TOO_MANY_BUFFERED_PARTS` and close connections with code 1008 under certain traffic patterns.

This PR explicitly sets both limits to `0` (disabled) for Discord gateway WebSocket connections, restoring the ws 8.20.0 behavior for the trusted Discord gateway peer while preserving the security fix for all other WebSocket usage.

## Changes

- **`extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway.ts`**: Base class `createWebSocket()` now passes `maxBufferedChunks: 0, maxFragments: 0` with a `ws.ClientOptions` cast (since `@types/ws` 8.18.1 does not yet expose these fields).
- **`extensions/discord/src/monitor/gateway-plugin.ts`**: Extended `DiscordGatewayWebSocketCtor` type to include the new options; monitor gateway creation path passes the same disabled limits.
- **`extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway.test.ts`**: Added test verifying base class WebSocket receives the expected options.
- **`extensions/discord/src/monitor/gateway-plugin.test.ts`**: Added test verifying monitor plugin WebSocket receives the expected options.
- **`extensions/discord/src/monitor/provider.proxy.test.ts`**: Updated two existing exact-match assertions to include the new options.

## Why `0` instead of raising the limits

- ws 8.21.0 treats `0` as disabled (`receiver.js:61`, `receiver.js:98`: `if (this._maxBufferedChunks > 0 && ...)`), matching the pre-8.21.0 behavior exactly.
- Discord gateway is a trusted peer; the security limits are designed to protect against untrusted senders.
- Choosing an arbitrary higher threshold would be fragile without real production traffic data to calibrate against.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: ws 8.21.0's retained-part receiver limits (`maxFragments` default 131072 / `maxBufferedChunks` default 1048576) abort a Discord gateway socket with `WS_ERR_TOO_MANY_BUFFERED_PARTS` / close `1008`; this PR sets both to `0` (disabled) on the Discord gateway sockets, restoring ws 8.20.0 behavior for that trusted peer.
- **Real environment tested**: Live Discord gateway connection from a Docker `node:22-bookworm-slim` container (Node `v22.22.3`) with the repo-pinned `ws@8.21.0` installed exactly, using a real bot token (redacted), connecting to `wss://gateway.discord.gg/?v=10&encoding=json`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**: build a `node:22-bookworm-slim` image with `npm install ws@8.21.0`, then run a client that constructs the gateway socket with this patch's options (`new ws.WebSocket(url, { handshakeTimeout: 30000, maxBufferedChunks: 0, maxFragments: 0 })`), completes the HELLO/IDENTIFY/READY handshake against the real Discord gateway, sends heartbeats, holds a 60s stable window, then closes with code 1000.
- **Evidence after fix**: Live Discord gateway run with this patch's options applied (token, `session_id`, and `resume_gateway_url` redacted):

```
[env] node=v22.22.3 ws=8.21.0
[discord] connecting wss://gateway.discord.gg (maxBufferedChunks:0, maxFragments:0)
[discord] open
[discord] HELLO heartbeat_interval=41250ms
[discord] IDENTIFY sent (token redacted)
[discord] READY received (session_id/resume_gateway_url redacted)
[discord] HEARTBEAT_ACK #1
[discord] stable window 60000ms complete
[discord] close code=1000 reason=<empty>
[result] PASS live: READY + 1 heartbeat ACK; no WS_ERR_TOO_MANY_BUFFERED_PARTS during stable window
```

Supplemental deterministic mechanism repro against a local ws 8.21.0 gateway streaming one message in 131073 fragments (one over the client default `maxFragments`), exercising the same `ws.WebSocket` receiver path:

```
# default ws.WebSocket (ws 8.21 defaults)
[before] open
[before] error code=WS_ERR_TOO_MANY_BUFFERED_PARTS message=Too many message fragments
[before] close code=1006 reason=<empty>

# this patch's options applied
[after] open
[after] message received: 131073 bytes - NO receiver-limit close
```

- **Observed result after fix**: On the real Discord gateway, with the disabled limits applied, the connection reaches `READY`, exchanges heartbeats, and stays connected through the 60s window with no `WS_ERR_TOO_MANY_BUFFERED_PARTS` and no `1008` close; the only close is the intentional client-initiated `1000`. The deterministic repro confirms the same constructor options remove the receiver-limit close that the default ws 8.21 client hits.
- **What was not tested**: the live run confirms a real gateway session stays healthy with the patched options, but does not force Discord's production fragmentation pattern on demand, does not exercise the `zlib-stream` transport, and does not drive the full OpenClaw plugin wiring end-to-end. The deterministic repro proves the ws 8.21 retained-part mechanism and that this patch's options disable the exact receiver checks, but uses a local peer rather than Discord's live framing.

## Tests

- `gateway.test.ts`: 25 passed
- `gateway-plugin.test.ts`: 17 passed  
- `provider.proxy.test.ts`: 21 passed
- TypeScript check (tsgo): clean

Fixes #88330

target.title: fix: add timeout to parent-fork token count resolution (fixes #101718)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveParentForkTokenCount` reads the parent transcript to estimate token count when forking a session, but has **no timeout or abort signal**. On large transcripts (hundreds of MB) or slow filesystems (NFS, FUSE, saturated SSD), this blocks session creation and reply fork paths indefinitely, accumulating blocked async contexts that exhaust gateway connection slots (#101718).

### Call chain

```
sessions.create({ fork: true })
  → session-create-service resolveParentForkDecision
    → session-fork.ts resolveParentForkTokenCount
      → session-fork.runtime.ts resolveParentForkTokenCountRuntime
        (fs.stat + async file read — NO TIMEOUT)
```

## Changes

**2 files, +54/-2 (source: +6; tests: +48)**

**`src/auto-reply/reply/session-fork.ts`** (+6 lines):
- Import `withTimeout` from `../../infra/fs-safe.js`
- Add `PARENT_FORK_TOKEN_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_000` constant
- Wrap `resolveParentForkTokenCountRuntime` in `withTimeout(..., 2_000).catch(() => undefined)`

When the 2-second timeout fires, `resolveParentForkTokenCount` returns `undefined` — the same sentinel the normal fallback path already produces. `resolveParentForkDecision` already handles `undefined` correctly: returns `{status: "fork"}` without `parentTokens` estimate.

This single bounded deadline (recommended by ClawSweeper review) covers all filesystem awaits inside the runtime (fs.stat + transcript read up to 1MB + potential index scan) in one wrapper.

**`src/auto-reply/reply/session-fork.test.ts`** (+48 lines):
- 3 new test cases for `resolveParentForkDecision`:
  1. Fast runtime → returns `fork` with `parentTokens` (50k)
  2. **Hanging runtime → returns `fork` without `parentTokens` within 2s** (timeout proof)
  3. Parent too large → returns `skip`

### Why 2 seconds and not 10?
- The timeout only guards the stale-token filesystem probe after the synchronous `freshPersistedTokens` fast path
- Even on NFS, fs.stat + 1MB tail read should complete in < 500ms
- 2s is aggressive but safe: returning `undefined` (allow fork without estimate) is always better than blocking indefinitely

## Evidence

```
   Start at  00:23:08
```

target.title: security(audit): flag control-plane exposure and plugin command surfaces
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two related gaps in `openclaw security audit` where operators could miss high-impact exposure on open chat surfaces and extension plugin command entry points.

### Gap 1: Control-plane tools on open inbound policy

When a channel uses `groupPolicy="open"` or an open DM policy, the exposure matrix flagged elevated and runtime/filesystem tools but did **not** separately flag **control-plane tools** (`cron`, `gateway`).

### Gap 2: Extension plugin commands on chat command surfaces

The plugin trust audit did not evaluate native command surfaces separately, name affected channels in finding detail, or warn when enabled extension plugins register commands reachable on those surfaces.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Control-plane exposure:** `collectRiskyToolExposureContexts()` now probes `cron` and `gateway`. Emits `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane` (critical) when open inbound policy can reach control-plane tools.

**Plugin command surface audit:** `collectPluginsTrustFindings()` adds `collectConfiguredCommandSurfaces()` and new/updated findings:

| checkId | After |
|---|---|
| `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` | critical when native commands **or** skill commands enabled without `plugins.allow`; detail names channels |
| `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` | warn when enabled extensions register commands and native commands are configured |

**Docs:** `docs/gateway/security/audit-checks.md` uses the correct `plugins.allow` config key.

## User Impact

* Operators get clearer findings when open chats can reach gateway/cron control or extension plugin commands.
* `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` may now report `critical` when native commands are active without `plugins.allow`.
* No runtime behavior change.

## Evidence

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
  src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts \
  src/security/audit-trust-model.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Open inbound policy could expose gateway/cron control-plane tools and plugin command surfaces without dedicated audit findings.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS (Darwin arm64), Node.js v22.22.0, local source checkout on branch `codex/audit-plugin-command-control-surface` (single commit on latest `main`).
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  1. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts src/security/audit-trust-model.test.ts --reporter=verbose`
- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ security audit trust model findings > evaluates trust-model exposure findings
   (includes security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane scenarios)
 ✓ security audit install metadata findings > evaluates install metadata findings
   (includes plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface scenarios)

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Production collectors `collectExposureMatrixFindings` and `collectPluginsTrustFindings` emit `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane` for open group + coding profile setups and `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` when enabled extensions register commands on configured native command surfaces.
- **What was not tested:** Full `openclaw security audit --deep` CLI against a live gateway; no committed `scripts/proof-*.mjs` helpers. Control-plane check ID overlaps with [#100965](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/100965) — maintainers should pick one canonical contract.

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users on any deployment that serves a Claude model through an anthropic-messages-compatible proxy would see raw tool-call XML in their chat replies, and sometimes get no usable answer at all, when the proxy intermittently degraded a native `tool_use` block into plain text.

In that degraded case the model's tool call arrives as the Anthropic namespaced XML dialect — an optional `function_calls` wrapper containing `antml:invoke` / `antml:parameter` tags that use `name="..."` attributes (MiniMax emits the same shape with an `mm:` prefix). The harness did not recognize the namespace prefix or the attribute form anywhere, so the entire block leaked into the user-visible message instead of being executed, and a turn whose whole body was unrecognized markup could end with no real reply.

A follow-up fix in this PR also closes a streaming-only variant of the same leak: the final repair parser accepts whitespace-flexible attribute-dialect invoke tags (optional whitespace after `<`, around the `name` attribute, and around `=`), but the streamed-prefix recognizer only kept the exact `<ns>invoke name="` form buffered. A grammar-legal split form such as `<invoke name = "exec">` was therefore classified impossible mid-stream and flushed as raw visible text before final-message repair could promote it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user: it should either be executed or, failing that, hidden. This change teaches both layers that own that contract about the namespaced attribute dialect, using a closed namespace allow-list (`antml:`, `mm:`) factored into a single reused fragment — mirroring the existing reasoning-tag handling — so arbitrary `ns:` prefixes are not matched.

- Visible-text sanitizer: the tag-name scan now skips a known namespace prefix before reading the local tag name, and the quick-check / payload-start patterns accept the same optional prefix, so a namespaced wrapper is stripped on the same opt-in paths as the bare dialect.
- Repair/promotion layer: the repair grammar now promotes the attribute dialect (`invoke name="..."` / `parameter name="..."`, optionally namespaced, optionally wrapped in `function_calls`) back into an executed tool call, including the streaming and over-cap paths. Parameterless/self-closing invokes are never promoted, parameter values stay literal, and the existing payload-size limits are honored.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: `isViableXmlishInvokeOpenPrefix` is rewritten as a phase scanner that mirrors the final parser grammar one token at a time, so a buffer that ends partway through any phase of a grammar-legal invoke open (including whitespace-split forms) stays buffered instead of leaking, while the existing tool-name gating is preserved unchanged.
- Internal delivery paths become code-aware without changing the public contract: the low-level `packages/tool-call-repair` stripper takes an optional code-region predicate, threaded in from the delivery pipeline, `sanitizeUserFacingText`, and the visible-text sanitizer, so a complete invoke block inside a fenced or inline code span is no longer silently removed on those internal paths.
- The exported plugin SDK helper `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` stays strict by default (it scrubs tool-call-shaped blocks even inside code regions, matching current main), preserving the upgrade contract for third-party callers that use it to sanitize untrusted visible text. Code-aware behavior is available as an explicit opt-in via `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }`; the default remains a strict scrubber.

Non-goals/boundaries: the Anthropic and DSML transports are intentionally untouched (the native path is correct; the failure is degraded text owned by the repair package and sanitizer); the exported SDK helper's default behavior is unchanged from main (strict), with code-awareness added only as an opt-in and to internal delivery call sites; and no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced. The equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude routes no longer see raw `antml:` tool-call XML in their replies. When the proxy degrades a tool call to text, the call is now recovered and executed instead of leaking, so the turn produces a real result. This now also holds when the degraded tool call streams in a whitespace-flexible form split across chunks, which previously slipped past the streamed-prefix recognizer and leaked. Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped.

## Evidence

Focused unit tests cover both layers and the edge cases:

- Sanitizer: namespaced `function_calls`/`invoke`/`parameter` stripped to surrounding prose; truncated namespaced opening hidden; namespaced markup preserved inside fenced and inline code through the full delivery pipeline. Delivery-path regression coverage locks both directions across the `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare (no-namespace) prefixes: an unfenced standalone `invoke` block (and a pure standalone block with no surrounding prose) is stripped, while the same block inside a fenced code span is preserved verbatim, so the real leak shape is removed without over-scrubbing legitimate code examples.
- Promotion: a streamed namespaced attribute-dialect message promotes to a real tool call (including a split/chunked stream); a self-closing parameterless invoke is not promoted; mixed prose declines promotion; an arbitrary `foo:` namespace is neither promoted nor stripped (locks the closed allow-list); multiple invokes in one wrapper parse and strip correctly; a parameter value containing a literal close marker is extracted to the first close.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: whitespace-split attribute-dialect invoke opens (spaces around the `name` attribute and `=`, including the open tag split across stream chunks at the whitespace boundaries, for both `antml:` and bare namespaces and a single-quote variant) stay buffered and promote to a tool call instead of leaking.
- Argument-less invoke followed by prose: a complete zero-parameter (`<invoke name="read"></invoke>\nHello`) or self-closing (`<invoke name="read"/>\nHello`) invoke followed by visible prose no longer leaks the raw invoke XML in streamed output — the invoke markup is stripped and only the prose (`Hello`) is delivered, with no tool call promoted, across `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare prefixes and split-across-chunks streams. Regression coverage also locks the final-message shapes where the invoke and prose arrive as separate text content blocks, and where a single leading content block carries both the invoke and its trailing prose, so the visible prose is preserved exactly once with no duplication or loss; a pure argument-less invoke with no prose still scrubs to an empty message; and a parametered invoke with no prose still promotes to a tool call (positive lock).

Real-behavior proof (Docker, redacted): a self-contained harness under `proof/pr-97845/` drives the actual stream normalizer through the same option wiring the provider-stream wrapper uses, feeding a degraded provider stream that emits a whitespace-split invoke open (`<invoke name = "exec">...`) split across chunks at the whitespace boundaries. Captured runtime output shows the regression and its fix:

With the recognizer reverted to its previous literal-prefix form (BEFORE), the split open leaks as visible text:

```
fake upstream chunks: ["<invoke"," name"," ="," \"exec\">","<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>","</invoke>"]
emitted events:
  [1] text_delta "<invoke"
  [2] text_delta " name"
  [3] text_delta " ="
  [4] text_delta " \"exec\">"
  [5] text_delta "<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>"
  [6] text_delta "</invoke>"
  [7] toolcall_start ...
visible text emitted to user: "<invoke name = \"exec\"><parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter></invoke>"
VERDICT: LEAK
```

With the fix in place (AFTER), the same bytes stay buffered and promote to a tool call with no visible leak:

```
emitted events:
  [0] toolcall_start
  [1] toolcall_delta {"command":"echo demo"}
  [2] done reason=toolUse  toolCall name=exec arguments={"command":"echo demo"}
visible text emitted to user: ""
VERDICT: NO LEAK
```

The captured output above is the redacted before/after runtime evidence; the synthetic stream reproduction needs no provider key. (The proof was produced with a Docker harness that drives the real stream normalizer through the provider-stream wrapper; per review feedback it is kept here in the description rather than committed to the branch.)

Exported SDK helper contract (strict default): the `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` tests lock both modes — with no options the helper strips a tool-call-shaped block even when it sits inside a Markdown code fence or inline span (strict scrubber, matching main), while `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }` preserves the same fenced/inline example verbatim. Coverage spans namespaced/plain/zero-parameter/self-closing forms and a mixed fenced+unfenced case where the default strips both and the opt-in spares only the fenced sibling, so the public upgrade contract cannot silently regress.

Local validation:

```
vitest src/plugin-sdk/tool-payload.test.ts: 50 pass (incl. dual-mode strict-default + preserveCodeRegions opt-in locks)
vitest src/plugin-sdk/provider-stream-shared.test.ts: 92 pass (incl. whitespace-split and argument-less-invoke-plus-prose regressions)
vitest src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts + src/infra/outbound/sanitize-text.test.ts: pass
node scripts/check-plugin-sdk-subpath-exports.mjs: OK
pnpm plugin-sdk:api:check: OK (baseline regenerated for the additive signature change)
pnpm tsgo:core: clean
git diff --check: clean
```

target.title: fix: strip volatile output from exec result hash to fix no-progress detection (#93917)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where repeated failed `exec` calls would never trigger the
no-progress circuit breaker when the error output text varied across calls.
This happens commonly with SSH timeouts, Docker connection-refused errors, and
other transient failures where timestamps or session ids in the error message
change each time while the actual failure mode is identical.

Fixes #93917

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/agents/tool-loop-detection.ts:196-246` | Split `hashExecToolOutcome`: `completed` keeps output; `failed` strips volatile text but preserves `{status,exitCode,timedOut,failureKind,exitSignal}` with numeric signal normalization via `normalizeExitSignal()` |
| `src/agents/tool-loop-detection.test.ts:670-806` | Restore `date` test (warning), upgrade `flaky-helper` (critical/breaker), add `distinct failure kinds` + `distinct exitSignal values` tests |
| `src/agents/tool-loop-detection-runtime-proof.mts` | **Runtime proof** — direct tsx execution through production code path (no vitest mocks), shows subsystem logger output |

## Why This Change Was Made

Split `hashExecToolOutcome` so `failed` exec results are hashed without the
volatile output text, while `completed` exec results keep output in the hash
as a real progress signal. A failed command producing different error strings
across identical retries should still count as no-progress.

## User Impact

Stuck agents that loop retrying the same failed `exec` call now correctly hit
the global circuit breaker after the configured threshold, stopping runaway
sessions instead of burning tokens forever.

## Evidence

### Runtime proof (direct Node.js, no vitest)

`src/agents/tool-loop-detection-runtime-proof.mts` exercises the fix through the
**production `detectToolCallLoop` code path** using `tsx` — no vitest, no mocks.
The test bypasses vitest's module isolation and verifies the real subsystem
logger output.

**Real environment:**
- OS: Linux x86_64, kernel 4.19.112
- Runtime: Node.js v24.13.1, tsx v4.22.3
- Commit: `204c3bd9`

**Exact command:**

```

```

**Full terminal output:**

## What Problem This Solves

Running `openclaw exec-policy show` or `openclaw approvals get` to inspect effective exec policy shows config + host approvals state, but **not** per-session `/exec` overrides set in an active chat or cron session. Nothing in the CLI output or docs mentioned this gap.
